analytic.title: Preemptive Phased Execution Models with Scratchpad Memory Requirements

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: There is currently a widespread interest in using phased execution models in the design of real-time systems, stimulated by their ability to reduce contention in accessing shared resources. The main beneficiary of such approaches is the wide category of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) multi-core systems, where complexity is an underlying issue. However, the advantage of predictability comes at a cost, which often resides in the additional decisions that are usually made when using phased execution models. One such decision is employing non-preemptive scheduling; as is well known, this leads to NP-hardness for most instances of the scheduling problem, while preemption can avoid this level of complexity in many cases. It is no surprise, then, that recent efforts have attempted to explore the possibilities offered by preemptive scheduling in combination with phased execution models.

Unlike existing work, the current paper focuses on the scratchpad memory consumption in preemptive phased execution models. The starting point, the model introduced by the authors of a previous article, was meant for the general analysis of the efficiency of preemptive scheduling in phased execution models. Notably, two methods for handling intermediate data are introduced, namely, the Waiting Time Minimizing Preemption (WMPM) and the Overhead Minimizing Preemption (OMPM). The current paper analyses the requirements of each approach in terms of scratchpad memory. It also introduces a hybrid method, in order to achieve a finer balance between memory consumption and schedulability constraints.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Phased execution models have emerged as a response to the challenges raised by the growing complexity of real-time systems. The complexity of the problems approached today and the costs incurred by the hardware implementations have lead to the arrival of the Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) multi-core platforms, which come with an efficient trade-off between performance and cost. The downside is that such a system treats the main memory as a shared resource, and handling the access to this resource becomes more and more complex as the number of cores and tasks increases [1]. The immediate response would be the use of cache memories. However, caches have a negative impact on predictability, which has resulted in a marked preference for employing local memories instead of cache memories [2].

As in most cases, dealing with complexity is easier when the different categories of actions are separated. Here, separation is about access to shared resources, namely, the global memory. The phased execution models, the best known of which are Acquisition-Execution-Restitution (AER) [3] and PRedictable Execution Model (PREM) [4], split the total execution time of each task into several phases, where each phase has clearly defined responsibilities with respect to the access to shared resources. The most obvious solution is the 3-phase approach, represented, for example, by AER and by 3-phase PREM [5], which will be considered during the rest of the paper. In this approach, the three phases of the execution of a task are: read, execute, and write.

To the best of our knowledge, there has been no attempt so far to systematically study the memory requirements and their impact on preemptive schedulability in phased execution models. First of all, non-preemptive scheduling has been preferred for phased execution models, to increase predictability [4], [6]- [9]. Only recently has begun preemptive scheduling to be considered being used with this model, given the difficult nature of the non-preemptive scheduling problem [10], which is known to be NP-hard for most of its instances [11].

The main reason for avoiding preemptive scheduling was the additional challenge in managing the local memory. On a COTS platform, during execution, a task relies on the code and data being stored on the local (scratchpad) memory. When preemption is used, the local memory must become available to the newly scheduled task. This can be achieved in two ways: either by removing the preempted task from the local memory, which requires a write-back operation to the global memory, with the inevitable contention and thus delays; or by ensuring that the local memory is large enough to host multiple tasks at once. Many research papers ignore the memory size problem [12]- [14]. When the issue is acknowledged, the authors rely on overly optimistic assumptions, such as each core having enough local memory space to fit all the tasks at once [15]. Such assumptions are still present in more recent works [16].

As an observation, the use of preemption might also introduce additional requirements for the global memory. When a task's execution is suspended, depending on the type of preemption used (see below), it may be necessary for the memory occupied by the task to be saved from the local memory to the global memory. This is not only about the instruction codes, which must be stored in the global memory in any possible model, but also about the task data. In practice, however, size limitations mostly refer to the local memory [17], and is the focus of the current paper.

In [18], the authors propose a dynamic iterative allocation algorithm for the scratchpad memory, in order to minimize the Worst-Case Response Time. The program is modelled as a Message Sequence Chart, which allows monitoring the interprocess contention. Although the technique is general and does not take into account the characteristics of the various existing execution models (such as the phased execution models), it opened a door in the analysis of scratchpad requirements. Other relevant contributions to the problem of scratchpad implementation can be found in [19]- [22].

A notable contribution has been brought by [17], which provides a detailed analysis of memory-related feasibility on scratchpad-based multi-core systems. The paper uses partitioned scheduling, where each task is modelled through a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The nodes of the DAG represent pieces of code that are executed sequentially, while the edges describe the precedence relations between the nodes. All tasks are considered as sporadic. Separating each task into a set of sequences does not contradict the basic structure of the phased execution model. However, the fact that each node is executed in a non-preemptive manner only allows a limited degree of preemption on the overall task execution, so it cannot be used directly for studying preemptive phased task execution.

A recent work [23] is finally bringing to attention the analysis of preemption in phased execution models. Because the paper is focused on preemption techniques, is touches only briefly the problem of memory size, but it sets up a general frame for assessing schedulability in such models. Very important, the paper defines two preemption methods, namely the Waiting time minimizing preemption and the Overhead minimizing preemption. The efficiency of the two methods is compared extensively, by varying numerous parameters such as: CPU utilization, number of tasks, number of cores, etc. In addition, a heuristic technique, named Schedulability Aware Preemption Heuristic, is proposed to help increase the degree of schedulability.

The current paper uses much of the general frame proposed in [23]. Our contribution consists in: the introduction of a new preemption method; an alternative schedulability heuristic; and a schedulability analysis for all preemption methods, considering the constraints of scratchpad memory size.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the model under which discussion is carried out. Section III revisits the preemption methods proposed in [23] and introduces the new method. Section IV shows the experimental results in comparing the efficiency of the three preemption methods. Finally, Section V draws the conclusions and lays the ground for future work.

div.head: II. THE MODEL
div.p: The model assumes a set of n independent periodic tasks τ = τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , running on a system with m cores. There is a main memory, accessible to the cores through a common bus. Apart from the global memory, each core has a local scratchpad memory, which is used to store all necessary information (instruction codes, variables, stack) for executing the running task. The global memory stores the memory space of each task. Transfer between the global memory and the local memory of a core occurs in the following situations:

• when a task is first scheduled after system power-up, the instruction codes of the task are copied to the local memory • when a task's execution is suspended and the space occupied in the local memory must be evacuated to the global memory • when a task's execution is resumed and its memory space must be written back to the local memory of a core We make the observation that, depending on the type of preemption being used, sometimes a suspended task may not need to be saved to the global memory and then loaded back into the local memory. That happens in the case that its memory contents is preserved in the local memory upon suspension. This is one of the key decisions that have to be made about preemption.
For the sake of symmetry, we assume that all cores are identical and that all local scratchpad memories have the same size and response time.

Each task τ i consists of three phases. For simplicity, we use the AER terminology: during the Acquisition phase, the task's information (instruction codes and data) is copied from the main memory to the local memory of the core on which it has been scheduled; the Execute phase is responsible for running the task; in the Restitution phase, the task's information is written back to the global memory. No overlaps between the phases of a task are allowed, nor may there be any inversion in the order of the phases. The main consequence of these constraints, and in fact the goal behind the model, is that during the Execute phase the task does need to access the global memory, thus it is not subject to the overhead incurred by bus arbitration.
A task τ i is described as
div.formula: (T i , R i , D i , M i , CA i , CE i , CR i ),
div.p: where:
div.formula: • T i is the task period • R i is the task release time • D i is the task deadline, with D i ≤ T i • M i is the worst-case memory consumption of the task • CA i , CE i ,
div.p: and CR i are the worst-case execution times of the three phases of the task, respectively Naturally, it is possible to compute the worst-case execution time of the whole task as C i = CA i + CE i + CR i . However, in most cases it is more useful to view separately the three phases, each with its own execution time.

As the tasks are independent, each task has its own period, not depending of the others tasks' periods. In order to charac-terize the periodical behavior of the whole system, the system hyperperiod is defined as the least common multiple of the periods of all tasks in the task set. Because the behavior of the system repeats itself from one hyperperiod to the next, in order to decide whether there is a feasible schedule for a task set, it is enough to analyze the schedulability for one hyperperiod. In other words, if all tasks, with all their instances within a hyperperiod, meet their deadlines, then the task set is schedulable for an unbounded number of hyperperiods.

div.head: III. PREEMPTION TYPES
div.p: While non-preemptive execution is straightforward, preemption can be implemented in various ways. For example, in the case of the phased execution models, one natural restriction is that a task cannot be preempted while in the Acquisition or the Restitution phase. Although preemption could be allowed throughout the whole duration of a task, there is an obvious rationale for enforcing such a limitation: suspending a task that is in the Acquisition phase means that all the information already transferred is lost, thus resulting in wasted time with no benefit; on the other hand, a task that is in the Restitution phase is already saving its information to the global memory, so interrupting that process in order to carry out another transfer (corresponding to another task) does not make sense.

In multi-core systems, there is also the issue of core affinity for the tasks, that is, if a task has already executed in part on a certain core before being preempted, after resumption one can impose the restriction of always scheduling it on the same core, or one can allow scheduling on any available core. Each of the two approaches has its advantages and drawbacks; what is important to mention is that the two methods result in very different ways of managing the local memories of the cores.

Based on this distinction, two methods to preempt execution phases have been proposed in [23]. We will briefly describe the two methods, and then we will introduce a compromise approach, which aims at preserving the advantages of both variants.

div.head: A. Existing Types of Preemption
div.p: The Waiting Time Minimizing Preemption Method (WMPM)

The goal of this method is to minimize the time that a preempted task has to wait until it can be scheduled again. This waiting time is due to the other tasks using the necessary computational resources, namely the cores and the global and local memories.

The flexibility required for minimizing the waiting time is achieved by allowing that any preempted task may be scheduled again on any core available. Consider an arbitrary task τ i , which had executed previously on core C k , but was preempted at some point. Since the task currently running on core C k might have a higher priority (which could be the very cause that τ i was preempted in the first place), then τ i might have to wait a long time before it can be scheduled again on C k , while other cores might execute tasks of lower priority.
WMPM is designed to avoid this kind of situation, by allowing τ i to preempt a lower-priority task running on any core.

The cost incurred by applying WMPM comes from the fact that scheduling a task on a new core assumes that the memory of that core is certainly available. Besides, this kind of task migration is only possible if all task information can also be copied into the local memory of the new core. In order to comply with these two requirements, whenever a task is preempted, its information is copied back to the global memory; similarly, when the task is scheduled again, its information is copied from the global memory to the local memory of the newly assigned core.

Apart from minimizing the waiting times of higher-priority tasks, WMPM has the obvious advantage of the lowest local memory consumption. Indeed, for the system to work, the size of the scratchpad memory of each core must only be large enough to host the information of the biggest task. The drawbacks come from the intensive usage of the global memory. Each time a task is preempted, an intermediate write operation to the global memory occurs. At the other end, each time a preempted task is scheduled again, an intermediate read operation occurs from the global memory to the local memory of the core allocated to the task. The intermediate operations are actually additional memory accesses, which would not be necessary had the task been preserved in the local memory of the previous core. Needless to say, additional memory operations could increase to risk of a task not meeting its deadline, so the schedulability of a task set could be affected.

Another element to be considered is the global memory consumption. In a multi-core system it is likely to have multiple preempted tasks simultaneously, whose codes and data are stored in the global memory at the same time. As shown in [23], for a system with m cores, on which a set of n tasks must be scheduled, the worst-case global memory consumption is equal to the sum of the sizes of the largest (n -m + 1) tasks. However, since the scratchpad memory consumption is usually the item of interest, global memory size is not an issue.

div.head: The Overhead Time Minimizing Preemption Method (OMPM)
div.p: This method goes the other direction. Its goal is to minimize the overhead incurred by preemption, by eliminating the intermediate memory operations when possible. This can be achieved by implementing core affinity, that is, each task runs on the same core, regardless of how many times it has been preempted. As a consequence, for each task, its code and data are stored in the local memory of a single core and they are not removed when the task is preempted. Thus, there is no need for intermediate read or write operations, since the task information is always in the same place.

When using OMPM, the elimination of the intermediate memory operations reduces an important source of delay in the execution of the tasks. On the other hand, core affinity introduces a certain degree of inflexibility in scheduling the tasks, which may also have a negative impact on the schedulability of the task set. More important, OMPM has far higher requirements regarding the size of the local memory. It must be noted that, if the local memory of the cores is insufficient at some point for a new task, the schedule will fail, and there is no way around that, since the tasks cannot migrate from one core to another. The worst case consumption for the local memory of a core is the same as the worst-case global memory requirement in the case of WMPM, mentioned above; i.e., it is equal to the sum of the sizes of the largest (n -m + 1) tasks. Nevertheless, in practice the necessary local memory is lower than the worst-case, and the exclusion of intermediate read and write operations makes OMPM a very efficient preemption technique.

div.head: B. The New Preemption Type
div.p: The Affinity-Exception Preemption Method (AEPM)

While both WMPM and OMPM have their specific shortcomings, it is worth exploring the strong points of the two methods. In short, WMPM is flexible in allowing any task to be assigned to any core. On the other hand, OMPM reduces the overhead incurred by resource access. Unfortunately, their goals are opposite, in the sense that each one is bringing an improvement in one direction at the expense of degrading the efficiency in the other direction. Thus, a compromise solution could get better results.

The experimental analysis carried out in [23] has demonstrated that OMPM is more effective than WMPM in most cases, so any attempt to put together the two methods should start from this fact. Thus, a hybrid preemption method should stick to the principles of OMPM, while reducing the high local memory consumption.

The new method, which we have called the Affinity-Exception Preemption Method (AEPM), behaves like OMPM in most cases, by preserving the core affinity of the tasks. The only exception occurs when the local memory of a core becomes insufficient to store the code and data for all the tasks assigned to that core. In that case, it is allowed to remove the information of a task from the local memory, by writing it back to the global memory. Later, when the task whose information was removed is scheduled again, its information is copied from the global memory to the local memory. The behavior of AEPM is depicted in Fig. 1.

In Fig. 1, the execution phases of the tasks are named using the AER convention. Task τ i has started running on core x and has completed first part of its execution phase (denoted as E i1 ), when preemption from task τ j occurs.

In case (a) of Fig. 1, the local memory of core x did not contain the information of task τ j and it is insufficient to copy it without removing another task. For the sake of simplicity, we assume that task τ i is the one removed, but the discussion would be similar if any other task was removed. Task τ j is copied from the global memory and starts running on core x. Later, when task τ i is scheduled again, it is scheduled on another core y; its information is copied to the local memory of core y and the task is completing the remainder of its execution phase (denoted as E i2 ).
We make the observation that a variant of the method could restrict the possibility of scheduling again task τ i only to the same core x.

Case (b) of Fig. 1 corresponds to one of the following situations: either task τ j was already in the memory of core x; or the local memory of core x has enough free space to allow copying task τ j . In that case, task τ i is not removed from the local memory, so later, when scheduled again, it will resume its executionon the same core x.

It is easy to notice that case (a) is similar to WMPM and case (b) is similar to OMPM. Indeed, in case (a) we see a second core involved, and also two additional (intermediate) memory phases for task τ i : a Restitution phase on core x upon preemption of task τ i and an Acquisition phase on core y upon resumption of task τ i . It should be noted that the AEPM method is designed to work efficiently under the following assumptions:
• for some (or all) of the cores, the local memory is smaller than the total amount necessary for the tasks scheduled on it • the situation corresponding to case (b) occurs only rarely;

if the local memory of a core is so small that removal to the global memory occurs often, the issue is similar to the phenomenon of thrashing encountered in virtual memory management, thus decreasing performance

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: The experimental setup is similar to that used in [23], with some differences given by the goal of the tests.

Most elements of the test data have been inferred from [24], which focuses on providing real-world values from the automotive industry. One of the most important pieces of information retrieved from [24] concerns the most widely encountered values for the task periods (1 ms, 2 ms, 5 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms, 50 ms, 100 ms, 200 ms, 1000 ms), together with their associated occurrence probabilities (3%, 2%, 2%, 25%, 25%, 3%, 20%, 1%, 4%). The task periods are used not only to compute the task set hyperperiod, but also in the generation of the task execution times. This is not done directly; instead, for each task, the random variable considered is the task utilization, which is generated as indicated in [25]. Given the utilization U i of task τ i , its execution time (WCET) is computed as
div.formula: C i = U i • T i .
div.p: Also, the amounts of memory required by the tasks are generated by using the label framework and the corresponding label distribution, described in the same paper [24].

Another contribution of [23] is the introduction of a new heuristic, designed to find an optimal balance between preemp-tive and non-preemptive scheduling. The Schedulability Aware Preemption Heuristic (SAPH) assigns a distinct status to each task, with two components: whether the task may preempt other tasks or not; and whether the task may be preempted by other tasks or not. SAPH consists of an iterative, trial and error process of attempting to find a feasible schedule of the task set; from one iteration to the next, the status of each task is updated based on its behavior (i.e., successful/unsuccessful scheduling) during the last iteration. Given the major increase in the performance reported in [23], we have employed it in our tests as well.

There are a few points where we move away from this experimental frame. Firstly, we use LLF-based scheduling [26] instead of EDF-based scheduling, which is used in [23]. We consider that, given the complexity of scheduling on multi-core systems and the overheads introduced by resource contention, LLF is better suited for such an approach.

Secondly and more important, our goal is to assess schedulability in the presence of local memory constraints. More precisely, we aim at comparing the various preemption methods that were described in the previous section, depending on the size of the scratchpad memory of each core.

There are two straightforward limits for a core's local memory. On one hand, the absolute lower limit is equal to the worst-case size of the largest task in terms of memory consumption (LT S): LT S = max i=1,n M i . As all cores are assumed to have the same size for the local memory, it is obvious that going below that limit would guarantee unfeasibility, because at least the largest task could never be scheduled on any core.

On the other hand, the obvious upper limit is equal to the sum of the worst-case sizes of all tasks. If each task has enough local memory space to accommodate all tasks at once, then memory would never be the cause for unfeasibility. It is still possible to fail in finding a feasible schedule due to some tasks missing their deadlines, but not due to memory shortages. While complying to the lower limit is actually the only requirement for the WMPM technique, we remind that WMPM introduces significant issues in finding a feasible schedule through the massive overhead caused by the intermediate transfers to and from the global memory. On the opposite side, OMPM eliminates this kind of overhead, but requires far more local memory (although the upper limit is unlikely to be needed in practice).

Our AEPM preemption method is trying to find an optimal balance between the two previous techniques. In order to assess the efficiency of AEPM, we have considered for testing various sizes of the cores' scratchpad memory. As the upper limit mentioned above is too pessimistic, we decided to use for the tests an upper bound related to the average memory load per core. For a system with n tasks running on m cores, the average memory load per core (ALC) is computed as ALC = ( n i=1 M i )/m. Because tasks may not be distributed uniformly to the cores according to their memory sizes, local memory size is varied from LT S to 150% • ALC, with steps of 10% of the length of the interval (150% • ALC -LT S). This way, we aim at capturing the changes in the performance of the scheduler as the size of the local memory varies between reasonable bounds.
Regarding AEPM, we consider two variants of it:

• A strong variant, which enforces the restriction that a preempted task, when resumed, may only be scheduled on the same core as before. • A weak variant, which allows a preempted task, when resumed, to be scheduled on any core. These two variants of AEMP are compared against the existing WMPM and OMPM techniques, under similar conditions.

Having set up the procedure, the tests are performed by employing various values for some relevant parameters: the task set total utilization; the number of cores available in the system; the number of tasks that make a task set. The values of those parameters mostly follow the experimental setup used by the authors of [23]. In addition, we introduce a new heuristic technique, similar in its goal with SAPH, which is used by default in our tests, but is highly demanding from the computational point of view; the efficiency of the two heuristics is also compared.

div.head: A. Task Set Utilization
div.p: The total utilization per task set gets the following series of values: 0.1; 1.1; 2.1; 3.1.

The results can be seen in Fig. 2. Not surprising, as the utilization becomes higher, schedulability drops for all methods. In all cases, as expected, OMPM yields a poor performance for low memory sizes, but its efficiency increases as memory size grows and, in the end, it can compete against any other method. A trend can be observed here: the higher the total utilization of the task sets, the sooner (in terms of memory size) becomes OMPM a match for the other methods.

div.head: B. Number of Cores
div.p: In this test set, the number of cores in the system receives the values 2, 41, 6, and 8 (Fig. 3). We ignore the case of a single core, as we are interested in the way multi-core systems can handle the scheduling problem.

As would be expected, the comparison between the preemption methods is not much different from the previous subsection. This is easy to explain by the fact that a higher number of cores implies a larger amount of local memory, available on all cores. Again, OMPM starts worse for low local memory sizes, but then catches up with the others. One curiosity here is that, as the number of cores increases, more memory is necessary for OMPM to match the other methods in terms of schedulability. In our opinion, this can be explained by the fact that the flexibility in scheduling the tasks to the cores can be better exploited on a larger number of cores. This idea is supported by the observation that the strong variant of AEPM, the other method that preserves core affinity for the tasks, also requires more local memory to match the competition on more cores. We have varied the number of tasks per set, by using the following values: 5, 15, 25, 35, as can be seen in Fig. 4.

As in the case of varying the total utilization, schedulability is high for a very low value of the number of tasks, then drops as the number of tasks increases. However, in this case we The experimental results confirm two facts what were already known: firstly, that WMPM is not affected by the size of the core local memory, as long as the lower limit (LTS) is observed; secondly, that OMPM requires a higher amount of local memory, but once that is available, it outperforms WMPM. On the other hand, the introduction of the new preemption method, the AEPM, is justified.

As would be expected, the strong variant of AEPM does not yield a significant improvement. Although it does allow for each core to be used by tasks whose total memory requirements exceed the size of the local memory, the restriction on running the same task on the same core introduces obvious limitations, which result in a large number of preemptions and thus in a high overhead.

The weak variant of AEPM, however, has proved very effective in all situations. Although WMPM can perform better when total utilization is low and the size of the local memory is close to LTS, a slight increase in these values quickly leads to AEPM taking over. For high values of the local memory, this variant of AEPM competes on equal ground with OMPM and in some cases behaves even better.

div.head: E. A New Heuristic
div.p: While the SAPH has proved quite efficient throughout the tests performed in [23], it is very complex and timeconsuming, by repeating the attempt to find a feasible schedule and adjusting the status of each task. We propose a different heuristic, which is simpler to implement and less computationally expensive.

The new heuristic, called Granularity-based Preemption Heuristic (GPH), has in common with SAPH the idea that unrestricted preemption may not be efficient in finding a feasible schedule. However, GPH is following a different path, as its inspiration comes from partitioned scheduling [17]. The Execution phase of each task is split into sequences of equal length; preemption may occur only at the boundary between two sequences. For reasons discussed earlier in the paper, the Acquisition and Restitution phases may not be preempted.

Obviously, the sequence length provides a measure for the granularity of preemption. It is intuitive that each application may have a specific degree of granularity that is better suited for efficient scheduling. Just like in the case of SAPH, we propose an iterative process, during which the granularity is increased on each iteration, until a feasible schedule is found.

We make the observation that splitting the task into sequences is made on a timing basis, without any connection with the logical flow of the code. In other words, it is possible to split a loop in the middle. As long as the tasks in the task set are independent, the preemption points are not restricted.
To check the efficiency of GPH, we have used the same test frame to compare the performance of the two heuristics on all preemption methods. The results can be seen in Fig. 5.

The experimental results show that SAPH behaves better for all preemption methods and all local memory sizes. However, GPH comes consistently (and somewhat surprisingly) close behind SAPH in all cases. While there is no doubt on which heuristic technique provides higher schedulability, we remind that SAPH is very expensive with respect to computational requirements. Given that, GPH might be a reasonable alternative to SAPH when computational power is an issue. This paper studies the impact of the size of local memory on schedulability in phased execution models, running on multicore COTS. A new preemption method, AEPM, is proposed and compared against existing methods: WMPM and OMPM. Experimental results show that AEPM is more efficient for low sizes of local memory, and also behaves very well for larger sizes, where it matches the state-of-the-art OMPM.

As future work, we intend to extend the study to modelling the interaction of non-independent task sets in phased execution models. Another direction is to explore a possible mixing between preemptive phased execution and partitioned scheduling.
